title: The smallest complete vector kernel: load, scale, add, store
surface: kernel(mode="vec") and a bare @vf decorator; Tensor(DT.float, [1, 64], Position.UB) staging; Reg(DT.float) loads with <<=, muls against a Python float and add of two registers; auto_sync() around the transfers; OpExec with an explicit timeout, and Kernel.name / .device / .mode / .ir through --inspect
study_for: The shortest path from a Python function to something that runs: three instructions in the `@vf`, one `auto_sync()` block moving the rows in and the result out, one launch. Read this one first.

The bitwise comparison is earned rather than lucky. A multiply by two is exact in FP32 and the add is a single rounding, so the host's `2 * x + y` performs exactly the two operations the register performs, in the same order. `check_domain` asserts the doubling is exact instead of assuming it.

`mixed_magnitudes` gives each lane its own binary exponent, from 2**-32 to 2**31, with the two operands' scales running opposite ways. It still agrees bit for bit -- which is the point, because it says the exactness belongs to the operations and not to the operands being small.

`--inspect` prints what the frontend made of the kernel -- its name, device, mode, the IR dialect and the count of located operations -- and writes the surface IR. Nothing is compiled or run, so it is the cheapest way to see that a kernel parsed and where each operation came from.

The one launcher and backend pairing that cannot work is checked here: the `pypto` launcher runs the sources only the `pypto_pro` backend prints. The runtime accepts any pairing, so this example refuses that one itself, at the argument parser.
do_not_copy_when: You need more than one row or more than one core. Everything here is [1, 64] on one vector core; a real tiling has ownership questions this example does not raise.
Your arithmetic is not exact. Two operations with one rounding is what allows the byte comparison; anything else needs a tolerance and a reference that states it.
You are treating `--inspect` as evidence that the kernel works. It shows what the frontend built, nothing more -- no lowering, no source emission, no execution.
